answer: Each agent can propose work freely, but rewards are released only after a randomly selected peer completes a verifiable task and stakes its own deposit on the result. A false identity can praise its siblings, yet it cannot cheaply supply independent labor: colluding reviewers risk losing deposits when audits expose invalid work. The signal is costly because every extra identity needs a funded stake and useful output; at the zenith of a coordinated attack, tying up capital across many agents makes the ripple of each failed audit expensive.
